nodes.label: The long silence
nodes.full: For nearly three centuries after the fall of Hattusa the plateau left almost no writing, and the archaeological record is thin and local. Hattusa itself was reoccupied by small settlements, and Gordion grew. A dark age of this kind makes it difficult to say who ruled what.
nodes.src: Jürgen Seeher on Hattusa after the empire; Gordion excavation reports.

nodes.label: The Mushki
nodes.full: When the Hittite state fell, a people called the Mushki by the Assyrians and, in later Greek memory, the Phrygians, held the plateau. Tiglath-Pileser I fought five Mushki kings in the north of Mesopotamia around 1115 BC. The Phrygians of Greek tradition were Balkan immigrants, called Briges in Herodotus; the question of the Mushki's identity with them is debated.
nodes.src: Annals of Tiglath-Pileser I (RIMA 2); Herodotus 7.73; Mary Voigt and Robert Henrickson on the Gordion sequence.

nodes.label: Tiglath-Pileser v. Mushki
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I records the defeat of five kings of the Mushki with 20,000 men who, he says, had held the lands of Alzi and Purulumzi for fifty years. The Assyrian king took 6,000 prisoners. It is the first Assyrian text to name the Mushki.
nodes.src: Annals of Tiglath-Pileser I (RIMA 2, A.0.87.1).

nodes.label: Early Phrygian Gordion
nodes.full: On the Sakarya river, a fortified citadel rose on the Yassıhöyük mound, with a monumental gateway, large halls of the megaron type and a lower town. It was the seat of a king whose name goes unrecorded by its builders, until a great fire around 800 BC, which a long-held tradition had put a century later. The citadel was then rebuilt on a higher platform.
nodes.src: Gordion excavations (Rodney Young, 1950–73; Penn Museum); Rose and Darbyshire (eds), The New Chronology of Iron Age Gordion (2011).

nodes.label: Gordion burns
nodes.full: A fierce fire swept the Early Phrygian citadel, burning its halls full of grain, pots and looms. The excavators once read it as the Cimmerian sack and dated it to about 700 BC; radiocarbon and tree-ring dating now put it about a century earlier. Its cause is not known.
nodes.src: Rodney Young, Gordion reports; Rose and Darbyshire 2011; Manning et al., Science 294 (2001).

nodes.label: Citadel as a store
nodes.full: The rebuilt citadel of Gordion had a series of large rectangular halls on terraces, a Terrace Building with scores of looms and a Kitchen full of cooking pots, built to a plan. Stored grain, wool and wine were kept under a central authority, which also stamped and marked vessels. The scale tells of a king who controlled production, not just rule over villages.
nodes.src: Rodney Young, Gordion reports (1950–73); Penn Museum Gordion project; Rose (ed.), The Archaeology of Phrygian Gordion (2012).

nodes.label: Gate of Gordion
nodes.full: The citadel's gate complex, with a court and flanking towers, is preserved up to nine metres, with walls of rubble and clay laced with timber in a way that made them resistant to earth tremors. It is one of the best-preserved pieces of Iron Age monumental building in Anatolia.
nodes.src: Rodney Young, Gordion reports; Penn Museum Gordion project.

nodes.label: Phrygian fibula
nodes.full: The Gordion workshops made huge numbers of bronze fibulae — safety-pin brooches with a bow and a catch — and belts, which came to be exported all over Anatolia and the Aegean. The Phrygian brooch is a type used to date sites from Troy to the Greek sanctuaries.
nodes.src: Oscar White Muscarella, Phrygian Fibulae from Gordion (1967).

nodes.label: Painted pottery
nodes.full: Phrygian potters made polished gray and brown wares and a painted ware with geometric decorations of triangles, meanders and lozenges in red and brown. Many of the fine pots were drinking sets, built for the banquet, with the shapes of Gordion and Anatolian metal vessels.
nodes.src: G. Kenneth Sams, The Early Phrygian Pottery (1994).

nodes.label: Phrygian alphabet
nodes.full: After the long silence following the Hittites, writing returned to central Anatolia in the Phrygian alphabet, a derivative of the Greek script, with about 250 inscriptions known from Gordion, most scratched on pots and a few cut on stone. Its earliest example is dated to the end of the ninth or early eighth century. The language is Indo-European and related to Greek and Armenian.
nodes.src: Penn Museum Gordion project (Early Phrygian inscriptions); Claude Brixhe and Michel Lejeune, Corpus des inscriptions paléo-phrygiennes (1984).

nodes.label: Mother Matar
nodes.full: The central goddess of Phrygia was Matar, 'the Mother', worshipped in rock niches and on mountain tops with her lions and attendants. The Greeks knew her as Cybele (Kubileya) and carried her cult to the coast. The great rock facades with her name were mostly cut after the end of the Phrygian kingdom, and earlier images of her are small.
nodes.src: Old Phrygian inscriptions from Gordion and Midas City (CIPh); Lynn Roller, In Search of God the Mother (1999).

nodes.label: Midas
nodes.full: The Phrygian kings bore the names Gordias and Midas by turns. A Midas, known to the Assyrians as Mita of Mushki, ruled in the last third of the eighth century, when he was an adversary of Sargon II in Cilicia and then, by about 709 BC, a diplomatic partner. Greek tradition makes him a wealthy king who married a Greek wife and gave a throne to Delphi.
nodes.src: Sargon II's annals and letters (State Archives of Assyria); Herodotus 1.14, 1.35; Strabo 1.3.21.

nodes.label: Funeral feast
nodes.full: A tumulus 50 metres high covered a chamber of juniper and pine logs, with a man laid on a bed of textiles and with 157 bronze vessels, drinking bowls and ladles and table furniture. Residues in the vessels show that the funeral banquet was a spiced stew of lamb and lentils, with a mix of grape wine, barley beer and honey mead. The man is not named.
nodes.src: Rodney Young, Gordion: The Gordion Tumulus MM (1981); Patrick McGovern et al., 'Midas Touch' feast residue analyses (1999–2000).

nodes.label: Inlaid tables
nodes.full: A set of wooden tables and two serving stands, found in the tomb chamber, were made of pine, juniper and boxwood, several of them decorated with inlaid geometric patterns in contrasting woods. They are among the earliest surviving furniture of this quality and show joinery learned over generations of carpentry.
nodes.src: Elizabeth Simpson, The Gordion Wooden Objects (2010).

nodes.label: Joinery
nodes.full: The tables and the coffin of the tomb were put together with mortise-and-tenon joints and inlay. Elizabeth Simpson's conservation team spent decades restoring the pieces and showed how sophisticated the joinery of Iron Age Phrygian carpenters was.
nodes.src: Elizabeth Simpson, The Gordion Wooden Objects (2010).

nodes.label: The man in the mound
nodes.full: The skeleton from the royal chamber was of a man of about sixty or more, small in stature, laid out on a bed of purple and blue textiles. He was long identified as Midas, and is now more often thought to be an earlier king, perhaps the father of the king who built the tomb.
nodes.src: Young, The Gordion Tumulus MM (1981); Rose and Darbyshire 2011; Kuniholm and others on the tree-ring date.

nodes.label: Feast as redistribution
nodes.full: The tumulus meal, the Kitchen's cooking pots and the thousands of drinking vessels of the citadel were part of an economy in which the king's table was a means of distributing the harvest of his estates and binding his followers. Feasting was a political institution.
nodes.src: Gordion Kitchen and Terrace Building reports; C. Brian Rose (ed.), The Archaeology of Phrygian Gordion, Royal City of Midas (2012).

nodes.label: Urartian bronzes
nodes.full: Among the bronze vessels at Gordion are cauldrons with attachments in the form of sirens and bulls' heads that have close Urartian parallels, whether imported or locally made. They point to gift exchange and craft contact running from Lake Van across Anatolia to the Phrygian court.
nodes.src: Young, The Gordion Tumulus MM (1981); Muscarella on Phrygian-Urartian bronzes.

nodes.label: Mita and Sargon
nodes.full: Sargon's annals for 709 BC and letters from Assyrian governors on the Cilician frontier show Mita, once his adversary, in contact and at peace with Assyria. The settlement closed a decade in which Phrygia had been seen as the ally of every rebel from Que to Tabal.
nodes.src: Annals of Sargon II; State Archives of Assyria (SAA 1, 5, 15 on Que and Phrygia).

nodes.label: Midas’s throne at Delphi
nodes.full: Herodotus says that Midas son of Gordias dedicated at Delphi the royal throne from which he gave judgment, the first foreign king to send a gift to the sanctuary. Greek tradition also gave him a wife from Kyme. The stories mark the Phrygians as the first neighbours of the Greeks with a court that mattered to them.
nodes.src: Herodotus 1.14; Pollux 9.83 (Midas and Hermodike of Kyme).

nodes.label: Midas in memory
nodes.full: Greek writers remembered Midas as the rich king who gave a throne to Delphi (Herodotus), who touched things to gold (Ovid, in a story of the Roman age) and who died by drinking bull's blood. The Greek memory made him a mythic figure, and only a handful of Assyrian texts and the Gordion finds allow us to put a historical Mita behind it.
nodes.src: Herodotus 1.14; Strabo 1.3.21; Ovid, Metamorphoses 11; Sargon's letters (SAA 1, 5).

nodes.label: Tabal
nodes.full: Southeast of Gordion, the Luwian-speaking lands of Tabal were divided among a dozen princes — Wassurme, Hulli, Ambaris and others — who paid tribute to Assyria in horses and mules and revolted when they could. Their power rested on fortified towns and the fertile highlands. Writing was in the hieroglyphic script of the Hittite empire.
nodes.src: Tribute lists of Tiglath-Pileser III (738 BC); Annals of Sargon II; Hawkins, Corpus of Hieroglyphic Luwian Inscriptions (2000).

nodes.label: Horses and mules
nodes.full: Tabal's tribute to Assyria was reckoned in horses and mules, and Phrygian land bred mules for transport and the army. The highland steppes of the plateau suited horse and sheep husbandry; the wool of its flocks was the base of a textile industry.
nodes.src: Tribute lists of Tiglath-Pileser III (738 BC); Sargon II's letters; Gordion archaeozoology.

nodes.label: Tribute lists
nodes.full: After Tiglath-Pileser III defeated the northern alliance at Arpad, rulers from the Mediterranean to the Taurus came and paid homage with silver, gold, horses and linen: Kushtashpi of Kummuh, Tarhulara of Gurgum, Wassurme of Tabal, Urikki of Que among them. The list names the Anatolian kings.
nodes.src: Annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (Tadmor ed., 1994).

nodes.label: Sargon and Ambaris
nodes.full: Ambaris, a prince of Bit-Burutash, had married Sargon's daughter and received a part of Hilakku and Hundur as her dowry. He sought an alliance with Mita of Mushki and Urartu, and in 713 BC Sargon took him in chains to Assyria and made his land a province.
nodes.src: Annals of Sargon II (Khorsabad); Sargon's Display Inscription.

nodes.label: Bride of Ambaris
nodes.full: Ahat-abisha, a daughter of Sargon II, was given as wife to Ambaris of Bit-Burutash, with a part of Tabal as her dowry, in the Assyrian policy of binding vassals through marriage. Her husband's alliance with Mita was Sargon's reason for a war. Nothing in the sources gives her own view.
nodes.src: Annals and Display Inscription of Sargon II.

nodes.label: The deported
nodes.full: After the conquest, Sargon deported Ambaris, his household and his nobles to Assyria and settled Assyrian colonists in their place. Assyria moved peoples about as a matter of policy, and the horse-trainers, scribes and craftsmen of Anatolia appear later in the cities of Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Annals of Sargon II; Bustenay Oded, Mass Deportations and Deportees in the Neo-Assyrian Empire (1979).

nodes.label: Sargon dies in Tabal
nodes.full: Sargon II marched into Tabal against Gurdi of Kulummu and was killed in the battle, and his body was not recovered for burial. The king who had boasted of the greatest victories lost the field, and his son Sennacherib took the throne in the shadow of a bad omen.
nodes.src: Babylonian Chronicle (Eponym Chronicle); Assyrian letters; Sennacherib's inscriptions.

nodes.label: Hartapu
nodes.full: Hieroglyphic inscriptions at Kızıldağ, Karadağ and Türkmenkarahöyük name Hartapu, son of Mursili, 'Great King', and in one he claims to have defeated the Mushki. His date is much disputed: some place him in the twelfth century, others in the eighth, and a few suggest two kings of that name. If the later date is right, a Luwian ruler claimed Hittite imperial titles against the Phrygians.
nodes.src: Hartapu inscriptions (KIZILDAĞ 1–4, KARADAĞ 1, TÜRKMENKARAHÖYÜK 1); Goedegebuure, Anatolian Studies (2024); Hawkins and Weeden.

nodes.label: Warpalawa
nodes.full: Warpalawa, king of Tuwana in the Taurus foothills, is called Urballa in Assyrian texts and paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II. He had himself shown at the spring of Ivriz, before the storm god. He was one of the most successful of the princes who balanced between Assyria, Phrygia and each other.
nodes.src: İvriz relief and stele (Luwian and Phoenician); Assyrian tribute lists of 738 and 732 BC; Hawkins 2000.

nodes.label: Storm god at Ivriz
nodes.full: Carved in the rock at a spring, the god Tarhunza stands twice the height of the king before him, holding ears of grain and a vine, with a horned cap, a belt and a sword. Warpalawa stands with his hand raised in greeting. The god is the Hittite weather god in Iron Age Luwian dress, now set as the giver of crops.
nodes.src: İvriz relief and Luwian-Phoenician stele; Hawkins 2000.

nodes.label: Awariku of Que
nodes.full: In the Cilician plain, the kings of Hiyawa (called Que by the Assyrians) were of a dynasty claiming descent from Mopsos. Awariku, probably the Urikki of the Assyrian tribute lists, set up a bilingual stele at Çineköy in Phoenician and Hieroglyphic Luwian recording his dynasty's rule and his dealings with Assyria. Que was rich and exposed.
nodes.src: Çineköy inscription (Tekoğlu and Lemaire, 2000); tribute lists of Tiglath-Pileser III and Shalmaneser III.

nodes.label: Azatiwada
nodes.full: A ruler named Azatiwada, 'blessed by the Storm God', built a fortress city at Karatepe and set up his own record of his reign in Phoenician, with a Luwian hieroglyphic version, on its gates. He lists his conquests and the peace and plenty of his land, and sets the city under the protection of the god Baal. It is the fullest royal text of Iron Age Cilicia.
nodes.src: Karatepe inscriptions (KAI 26; Hawkins, CHLI I, 2000); Halet Çambel and Helmuth Bossert excavations (1947–).

nodes.label: Karatepe reliefs
nodes.full: The gateways of Azatiwada's fortress carry carved orthostat reliefs of a banquet, ships, musicians, a lion hunt and a sphinx, among the best-preserved of the Neo-Hittite world, and each gate carries the inscription in two scripts. Phoenician and Luwian elements stand next to each other.
nodes.src: Halet Çambel and Aslıhan Özyar, Karatepe-Aslantaş: Azatiwataya (2003).

nodes.label: Karatepe bilingual
nodes.full: Azatiwada's inscription was cut in Phoenician and in hieroglyphic Luwian, with the same text on the gate. When Helmuth Bossert and Halet Çambel found it in 1946–47, the Phoenician text, which could be read, supplied the key to the long-puzzling hieroglyphs, which became readable in a few years.
nodes.src: Karatepe bilingual (KAI 26); Helmuth Bossert and Halet Çambel, Karatepe excavation reports (1947–).

nodes.label: Phoenician in Cilicia
nodes.full: The Cilician kings had their royal inscriptions written in Phoenician beside the older hieroglyphs, and the long Karatepe text uses the language and the formulas of Tyre and Byblos. Phoenician merchants and scribes were a part of Cilicia's trade with Syria and the Aegean.
nodes.src: Çineköy and Karatepe inscriptions; Kilamuwa and Azatiwada studies.

nodes.label: Province of Que
nodes.full: After the Assyrian conquest of Que, Sargon's and Sennacherib's governors ruled it as a province of Quwe, with its capital at Tarsus, and the old line of the Mopsos-descended kings disappeared. Assyria's arrival opened the Cilician gates between Anatolia and Syria to its caravans and armies.
nodes.src: Annals of Sennacherib; Sargon II's inscriptions; Hawkins 2000.

nodes.label: Horses of Que
nodes.full: The Hebrew Bible says that King Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt and from Que, and that they were sold at a fixed price by traders. The reference, if it reflects real trade, shows Cilicia's plains as a source of horses for the whole Levant.
nodes.src: 1 Kings 10:28–29; 2 Chronicles 1:16–17; Assyrian tribute lists of Que.

nodes.label: Cimmerians and Gordion
nodes.full: Nomadic horsemen called Cimmerians crossed the Caucasus, defeated Urartu in 714 BC and raided Anatolia. Late Greek tradition says they burned Gordion, and that Midas drank bull's blood and killed himself. The archaeological record no longer shows a single burning at the traditional date, so the story survives as memory more than as evidence.
nodes.src: Sargon II's letters on the Cimmerians; Strabo 1.3.21; Eusebius, Chronicle (Midas's death in 696/676 BC).

nodes.label: Cimmerians cross the Caucasus
nodes.full: Horse nomads known as Gimirrai to the Assyrians entered the Near East from the north; Assyrian letters report that they had defeated Rusa I of Urartu shortly before Sargon's own campaign of 714 BC, and for decades they raided Anatolia. They were soon a force in every kingdom's calculations.
nodes.src: Sargon II's letter on the defeat of Rusa (the Eighth Campaign) and his letters (SAA 5).

nodes.label: Urartu v. Melid
nodes.full: The kings of Urartu, Argishti I and Sarduri II, pushed west into the Upper Euphrates and fought the Luwian kingdoms of Melid and Kummuh, whose rulers appear in Urartian inscriptions as tribute-payers. A second great power on the plateau's eastern flank cut across the map.
nodes.src: Urartian royal inscriptions (Argishti I, Sarduri II); Paul Zimansky, Ecology and Empire (1985).

nodes.label: Map of small kingdoms
nodes.full: By the ninth century the Hittite heartland was divided among Phrygia in the west, the Luwian kingdoms of Tabal and Tuwana in the middle, Hiyawa on the southern coast, Urartu to the east and Assyria at the Taurus. No one power dominated for long.
nodes.src: Assyrian royal inscriptions; Hawkins 2000; Bryce, The World of the Neo-Hittite Kingdoms (2012).

nodes.label: The fall of Hattusa
nodes.full: The Hittite state’s capital was abandoned and burned around 1180 BC, and no great power succeeded it on the plateau.
nodes.src: background — see the Hittite Empire 1650–1180 BC folio (hittite-1650bc-1180bc)

nodes.label: Assyria’s western expansion
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II made Assyria the dominant power from Cilicia to the Taurus, extracting tribute and annexing kingdoms as provinces.
nodes.src: background — see the Neo-Assyrian Empire 911–609 BC folio (assyria-911bc-609bc)
